title: Customer communication templates
summary: Five situations you will write for every week: acknowledging, asking for information, announcing a delay, saying no, and closing the loop with an apology when one is due.

lessons.title: Acknowledge, ask for information and announce a delay
lessons.body:
Good support writing is short, specific and honest about time. Use templates as skeletons, never as pasted blocks, and change the details every time.

**Situation 1: Acknowledge.** The goal is to show the report was read and say what happens next. Avoid an empty 'we received your ticket'.

> Hi Dana, thanks for reporting that the Tuesday shifts show an hour late for your Arizona pharmacists. I have logged it as DISP-401 and will confirm the cause by end of day tomorrow. Until then, please check those shift times in the dispatcher view.

**Situation 2: Need more information.** Ask the fewest questions that unlock the case, numbered, with an easy way to answer, and say why you ask.

> To reproduce this I need three things: 1) the shift id or pharmacy and the time you saw, 2) whether it happens in the web app, the phone app or both, 3) a screenshot of what you see. A reply to this email is enough. I will check back on Thursday.

**Situation 3: Delay or SLA at risk.** Tell the customer before the promised time passes. Give the new time and the reason in plain words, and what they can do now.

> I told you we would have an answer today, and I do not have one yet. The developer needs the logs from yesterday's alert run, which are being restored. I will update you by 15:00 tomorrow. If an urgent shift needs filling before then, call us and we will assign it.

**Rules that hold in all three.**

1. Greeting with the name, one clear purpose in the first sentence.
2. One request per message when you can; if there are several, number them.
3. Concrete times (Thursday 10:00), not 'soon'.
4. Avoid blame ('you did not'), internal terms ('Tier 2', 'backlog'), and over-promising.
5. Match length to the reader. A pharmacist on a phone reads three short lines.
6. Reread for tone. 'Unfortunately' and 'as I said before' read as cold.

**A quick test.** Read it as the customer: do I know what they will do next, and when I will hear again? If not, rewrite.
keyPoints: An acknowledgement states what you understood and what happens next, with a time.
Ask for information in a numbered list and say what a reply needs to look like.
Announce a delay before the promised time, with a new time.
Use concrete times and plain words.
lessons.interviewAngle: A practical test may ask you to write a reply. Show the structure: understood problem, next step, time, workaround. Your phone and email support work gives you real examples of wording that calmed people down. Keep a sample reply of your own to hand, with names and details removed, in case they ask for one.

exercises.prompt: You promised an answer by Wednesday and need until Friday. When do you tell the customer?
choices: Before Wednesday ends, giving the new time and the reason
exercises.explanation: Silence after a promised time damages trust more than the delay itself.

exercises.prompt: Which request for information is best?
choices: Can you tell me everything about what happened and your computer and the whole history?
To reproduce this I need: 1) the shift id, 2) web or phone app, 3) a screenshot. Reply to this email.
exercises.explanation: It is specific, short, numbered and easy to answer.

exercises.prompt: Write the acknowledgement for this email: 'Our pharmacists did not get the text for last night's emergency shift, and we had to call around. This is the second time this month!' Use the practice product, promise a next step and a time.
exercises.answer: Hi Jordan, I am sorry about the scramble last night. I understand the emergency shift alert did not reach your pharmacists and this is the second time this month. I have logged it as DISP-512 with high priority and am checking the alert log for last night's shift now. I will send you what I find by 12:00 tomorrow. If another urgent shift cannot wait, call our support line and we will assign it directly.
rubric: Shows the problem was understood, including the repeat
A short, real apology without excess
Names the reference and a next step
A time for the next contact and a workaround

exercises.prompt: Write the delay message: you promised a fix for the duplicate-assignment bug by Friday, but the developer found the fix also affects bulk upload and needs another test cycle. New date Tuesday.
exercises.answer: Hi Priya, an update on the duplicate assignments (DISP-388). I told you the fix would be ready Friday. While fixing it the developer found the same change affects bulk upload, and we need another round of testing to be sure we do not break that. The new date is Tuesday afternoon, and I will confirm by 10:00 that day. Until then, please avoid double-clicking Assign; one click is enough. I am sorry for the extra wait.
rubric: New date and a time to confirm

lessons.title: Saying no, and closing the loop
lessons.body:
The two hardest messages are the one that declines a request and the one that closes a ticket after a failure.

**Situation 4: Decline (feature request, not a bug, or won't fix).** Say no clearly, give the reason, give an alternative and say what you will do with the request. Never hide a no inside a long message.

> Hi Sam, thanks for asking for a way to bulk-upload shift requests (DISP-290). We will not build this in the next two quarters because it competes with work for emergency alerts, which affects more customers. I have recorded your request and your volume of about 60 shifts a week, which helps us rank it. In the meantime I can load your next batch from a spreadsheet for you. Would you like to send one?

Checks: the customer knows the decision, why, what you did with the idea, and what they can do now. A false 'we will look into it' only delays disappointment.

For a **'working as designed'** answer, explain the design and the reason, and ask what they were trying to do, which may reveal a real need.

**Situation 5: Resolution, and apology when due.** Tell the customer what was wrong, what changed, how to check, and that you will reopen if it recurs.

> Hi Dana, the Arizona time display problem (DISP-401) is fixed in version 2.3.3, released this morning. I checked Arizona, Mountain and Pacific shifts and they all show correctly now. Please look at next week's roster and tell me if anything still looks off; I will keep the ticket open until Friday. I am sorry the wrong times caused extra checking for your team.

**When to apologise.** Apologise when the company made a mistake or the customer lost time. Do it once, specifically, in the first or last sentence. Skip it when nothing was wrong (a how-to question). Do not apologise for the customer's feelings ('sorry you feel that way').

**Angry customers.** Acknowledge the impact in your first line, state what you can do, and avoid arguing with the tone. If the message is abusive, follow the policy and escalate. Do not reply while irritated: draft, wait, reread.

A closing checklist: reference number, what changed, how verified, what to do if it returns, thanks.
keyPoints: A decline states the decision, the reason, what you did with the request and an alternative.
A resolution message says what changed, how it was verified and how to reopen.
Apologise once and specifically, only when something was wrong.
For anger, acknowledge impact first and state what you will do.
lessons.interviewAngle: 'How do you tell a customer no?' is common. Use the four-part shape and give the example of declining a request while capturing it and offering a workaround. This fits your role between customers and developers. Never paste real customer details into an example; anonymise them first.

exercises.prompt: Which is the best way to handle a feature request you will not build soon?
choices: Say 'we will look into it' to keep them happy
Say no clearly, explain why, record the request and offer a workaround
exercises.explanation: A clear no with a reason and an alternative is more respectful and avoids repeated chasing.

choices: I am sorry you feel that way.
I am sorry the wrong times cost your team extra checking. That was our error.
Sorry, sorry, so sorry for everything.
exercises.explanation: A specific apology for a real impact, once, is credible. The first is dismissive and the third is excessive.

exercises.prompt: A pharmacy manager writes: 'Your system is useless. I asked three times for the export to include the pharmacist licence number.' This field is not in the export and there are no plans to add it. Write the reply.
exercises.answer: Hi Taylor, I can see you have asked three times and I am sorry we have not given you a clear answer. The export does not include the licence number, and we have no plans to add it in the coming months, because licence data is kept in a separate secure record. I have added your request to our product list with your use case, which helps us rank it. In the meantime I can send you a spreadsheet each month that matches pharmacist names to licence numbers from the secure record, if your account is authorised. Would that help?
rubric: Acknowledges the repeats and the frustration without defensiveness

exercises.prompt: Write the closing message for the duplicate-assignment bug fixed in version 2.3.4 and verified on staging. Include verification, how to check, how to reopen, and a short apology.
exercises.answer: Hi Priya, the duplicate assignments (DISP-388) are fixed in version 2.3.4, released today. I tested double-clicking Assign and bulk upload on staging, and each produced one assignment. If you see a pharmacist assigned twice to the same shift, reply to this email with the shift id and I will reopen the ticket. I am sorry for the duplicate texts your pharmacists received. I will close this ticket on Friday unless I hear from you.
rubric: How to check and how to reopen
